EU-ForDAM: gap-filling test and gap-filled dataset (v1)

PhD objective 1: harmonising incomplete records

Published

October 15, 2026

The question

Most gaps in EU-ForDAM are insects a country never reported. Following the thesis premise, the existing records carry information about the missing ones, we estimate those gaps from the insects that were reported. Rules: 0 = monitored, no damage (kept); not reported = unknown (estimated, never set to 0); host tree absent from the region = 0 (forest table of Hlasny et al. 2025); value1 only; the Czech spruce bark-borer group counted as I. typographus as in the paper.

How methods were tested

Real reported values were hidden in whole country x insect blocks (exactly the shape of a real gap: a country without any record of an insect), predicted from the rest, and compared with the truth: 17,351 hidden cells, 10 rounds. Insects reported by only one country cannot be tested this way.

Method What it does
Simple average the insect’s mean in that year (the yardstick)
Partner method borrows from insects linked to it (correlation metrics) recorded in the same region-year
Factor model latent factor model using all insects at once, in two parts: any damage? x how much?; each insect’s level pulled towards its broad group
+ forest area the factor model plus host-forest area per region (NUTS forest table)

method error per cell (log) damage vs no damage (AUC) totals within 2x typical total error (x off)
simple average 4.00 0.64 8% 45.70
partner method 3.77 0.68 11% 25.17
factor model 3.43 0.76 25% 4.60
factor model + forest area 3.57 0.72 26% 4.54
factor model + forest area (amount only) 3.41 0.76 25% 4.54

Result. Methods that use the other insects beat the simple average, which supports the thesis premise. The factor model is clearly best: it separates damage from no damage much better (AUC 0.76 vs 0.64) and gets regional totals far closer (typically 4.54x off vs 46x), because it learns each region’s overall level from all its other insects. Forest area adds only a little, and only when used for the amounts.

The best method differs by insect; the partner method wins for several conifer bark beetles with strong, consistent partners.

Attempts to improve further

method error per cell (log) damage vs no damage (AUC) totals within 2x typical total error (x off)
factor model (v1) 3.39 0.76 25% 4.54
recalibrated only 3.42 0.74 8% 26.96
+ memory 3.42 0.75 8% 26.63
+ neighbours 3.37 0.74 7% 34.91
+ reporting effect 3.44 0.74 8% 26.21
+ all three 3.39 0.75 7% 31.10
+ all three, Tweedie 5.06 0.73 22% 6.03

Memory (the region’s other insects last year), neighbouring regions (NUTS positions), a country reporting effect and a Tweedie distribution were added as a second stage. None beat the factor model: memory and reporting level are already captured by it through the other insects; neighbours carry a little extra information, but adding them as a second stage disturbs the level and damages totals. This suggests the model is close to what the damage records alone can predict; further gains likely need external drivers (drought/VPD, storms) and spatial structure inside the model.

The gap-filled dataset v2 (factor model only, with ranges)

Changes from v1: the same data as the correlation metrics (Czech spruce bark-borer group counted as I. typographus); the factor model only (no partner method); aggregate reporting codes are not filled; every filled total has an 80% range taken from the hide-and-predict test.

value_type confidence cells share
filled reliable 6561 8%
filled untested 14552 17%
filled weak 13672 16%
not fillable (nothing recorded in this region-year) NA 11898 14%
not filled: aggregate reporting code NA 7369 8%
reported damage NA 9828 11%
reported zero NA 17254 20%
zero: host tree absent NA 5645 7%

Ranges. The final model was re-run 10 times, each time with different country x insect blocks hidden. For every hidden country x insect x year total the real value is known, so the spread of real / predicted tells how far off a filled total typically is; its 10% and 90% points give the 80% range (per insect when it has at least 30 hidden totals). Check: learning the spread on half the folds, 74% of the other half’s real totals fall inside the 80% range (target 80%), so the ranges are slightly too narrow.

Confidence. Reliable = in the test, the model beats the simple average for that insect and separates damage from no damage (AUC >= 0.7): 10 insects (den_pin, dip_sp, geo_db, lym_dis, neo_ser, pan_fla, pha_cya, pis_pin, pit_spp, pol_pol). Weak = tested but not both: 23 insects. Untested = recorded in one country only; filled but left out of totals.

Caution. For several insects the filled damage is many times the reported damage (e.g. Ips duplicatus, Pissodes pini, Thaumetopoea pityocampa, Lymantria monacha). The model fills every region where the host tree grows and something was recorded, including countries outside an insect’s geographic range (the pine processionary moth is Mediterranean). A country x insect “could occur here” mask (range maps or expert judgement) is needed before Europe-wide totals are used.

How to read it

  • Reported values are untouched; every filled value carries its method and confidence.
  • Filled values are good for whether and when damage occurred, rough for how much (a single regional total is typically several times off).
  • Europe-wide totals: use reported + reliable fills; treat weak and untested fills as indications only.
